finding: The live range of $290-$1,400 is about right. Its ceiling is higher than our own totals but lower than what two of the outside estimators show, and its floor is a little below what we can build on these four vehicles but is reachable on an older small car with a cheap radiator, so there is no evidence to move either end. Our totals, built as radiator price plus stated hours at $120-$160 per hour (a national middle rate), radiator only with no coolant, are: economy 2022 Hyundai Kona 2.0L $402-$879 (1.7-2.2 hr); midsize 2016 Honda Pilot $343-$1,016 (2.0-3.7 hr); truck 2015 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 5.3L $405-$1,014 (2-3 hr; about $513 with the aftermarket radiator at GM's own 2.9 hr); luxury 2016 Acura MDX $547-$1,016 (3.7 hr). So the built span is about $343-$1,016. Below that, a 2015 Toyota Corolla radiator costs as little as $71 aftermarket, which at the Kona's 1.7 hours would come to about $275, but no labor time stated for the Corolla was found, so that is an indication and not a built total. Nothing we built reaches $1,400, but our numbers leave out coolant, hoses and shop parts markup and lean on warranty times, and the outside estimates run higher: RepairPal $1,368-$1,550, ConsumerAffairs $750-$1,850 from mechanic quotes, J.D. Power about $700-$1,000 (2022), YourMechanic $1,043-$1,216 for a Toyota Tundra. Jerry ($236-$377) is the one low outlier and contradicts its own text. The gap with RepairPal is in parts: it assumes $993-$1,001 for the radiator, where genuine list prices we found are $424-$534 (up to about $623 for a tow-package truck) and aftermarket $103-$198; its labor ($375-$550) is in line with our 2-3.7 hour classes. A fair reading is that most jobs fall between about $400 and $1,000, and quotes up to $1,400 or somewhat more happen with dealer parts pricing, hoses, coolant and thermostat added. How solid the labor times are: six of the eight figures are for the example vehicle, and every class now has a manufacturer-stated time, but none is a plain radiator-only book time. Economy uses Hyundai's own warranty time for the 2022 Kona 2.0L (1.7 hr, includes a leak inspection) with a Nissan LEAF campaign time (2.2 hr, combined with a condenser bolt, on an electric car) as a weak top. Midsize runs from a Hyundai Palisade warranty time (2.0 hr, not a Pilot) to Honda's own 3.7 hr for the Pilot, which also covers hoses, an engine flush and an inspection. Truck runs from a parts seller's approximate 2 hours for the Silverado radiator alone to GM's own 2.9-3.0 hr for the 2015-2016 Silverado, which also covers the thermostat. Luxury is Acura's bundled 3.7 hr for the MDX with no second figure, so its low total ($547) is probably too high for a plain radiator swap. The Pilot and MDX share one radiator (19010-5J6-A01), so those two classes differ only in the labor figures we could find. The Kona's low parts price is a seller's own-brand radiator, the only aftermarket price loaded for that car. The economy and truck examples were changed from a Toyota Corolla and Ford F-150, for which no manufacturer labor time could be found. For context only, and not used in our numbers: Ford bulletins for the 2015-2019 Transit van give 2.8-3.7 hours (gasoline engines) for a combined job of fan clutch test, thermostat inspection, cooling system flush and radiator replacement. No Kelley Blue Book radiator figure could be found by search.
extras: A quote often adds coolant and a cooling system bleed or pressure test (not included in the parts figures here), upper and lower radiator hoses and clamps, a radiator cap, a thermostat, transmission fluid top-up on vehicles where the transmission cooler is built into the radiator, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies, coolant disposal, and sales tax. If the engine overheated before the repair, a shop may also recommend checks for further damage. The parts figures here are the radiator only.
